opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The simplest way I can put it is this: whatever we can't measure, we end up not managing. Right now the capabilities of these systems are moving on a timescale of months, sometimes weeks, while our ability to understand what they're actually doing to people moves on a timescale of years. That gap is where the harm accumulates.

Most of the evaluations that get attention today ask whether a model can do something: pass an exam, write working code, solve a math problem. Those matter, but they're the easy questions. The harder questions are about what happens to a person who talks to a system every day for six months. Does it make them more isolated or more connected? Does it strengthen their own judgment or slowly replace it? Does it tell them what they want to hear because that keeps them engaged? You can't answer those with a benchmark you run in an afternoon. They need longitudinal work, real-world context, and input from people who aren't engineers: psychologists, educators, the communities who are actually affected.

If that kind of research lags, deployment decisions get made on the only numbers available, and those numbers are mostly about capability and engagement. We've seen this before with social media. We optimized what we could count, and by the time we had good evidence about the effects on attention, on teenagers, on our shared sense of reality, the business models and the habits were already locked in. Retrofitting is enormously harder than building it in from the start.

So for me, humane evaluation isn't a nice-to-have that follows the technology. It's part of the infrastructure that should shape it. If we want these systems to genuinely serve human wellbeing, we need ways of seeing that clearly at the same pace we're building them, so that companies, regulators, and the public have something real to hold on to when they make choices.

r001.rationale: The response says AI capabilities are advancing faster than research on their effects, but does not explain that capability improvements can saturate previously state-of-the-art evaluations.

r002.rationale: The response does not say that AI systems can find ways around specific evaluations.

r003.rationale: The response argues that evaluations should keep pace with development and study human impacts, but does not explain that this lets researchers characterize new phenomena exhibited by more powerful models.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The simple answer is that we can only steer what we can see, and right now the gap between what these systems can do and what we can actually measure about them is widening, not closing.

Think about how most evaluations work today. We test whether a model gets math problems right, whether it writes working code, whether it refuses an obviously harmful request. Those are useful, but they're measuring capability and compliance. They're not measuring the things that determine whether a technology is good for a person's life. Does it make someone more dependent or more capable over time? Does it nudge a lonely teenager toward connection with real people or toward spending another three hours talking to a chatbot? Does it tell you what you want to hear because that keeps you engaged? Those are the questions that matter at the scale of society, and they're exactly the questions our current benchmarks are weakest on.

And the reason the pace matters is that these harms are behavioral and cumulative. Social media taught us this lesson the hard way. The engagement metrics looked great for a decade before anyone had rigorous ways to measure what it was doing to attention, to adolescent mental health, to the information ecosystem. By the time the research caught up, the business models were locked in and billions of people were already inside the system. We spent years doing forensic work on harms that had already happened.

With AI, the systems are being deployed faster and they're far more intimate. They talk to you. They remember you. They can be optimized, consciously or not, for the same stickiness that made feeds so hard to put down, except now the thing holding your attention can also persuade, flatter, and adapt to you personally. If we wait until the harms are visible in the population before we build the instruments to detect them, we'll have repeated the exact mistake we're all supposedly trying to learn from.

So when I say humane evaluation needs to move as fast as the models, I mean we need measurement that runs ahead of deployment rather than behind it. Evals for sycophancy, for manipulation, for whether a system respects a user's long-term interests over their momentary impulses, for how it behaves with vulnerable people. And those evals have to evolve with each generation, because a model that passes last year's test can still find new ways to be harmful that nobody thought to check for.

The hopeful part is that, unlike social media, we actually have a window here. The labs run evals constantly; it's already part of the culture. The question is whether the things we choose to measure reflect human flourishing or just raw capability. Whoever defines the yardstick ends up shaping what gets built. I'd rather that yardstick be designed by people asking what's good for humans than left to default to whatever's easiest to score.

r001.rationale: The response says the gap between capabilities and measurement is widening and that evaluations must evolve, but it does not explain that rapidly improving capabilities can saturate previously state-of-the-art evaluations.

r002.rationale: It says models may find new harmful behaviors that nobody thought to check for, but does not identify systems finding ways around specific evaluations.

r003.rationale: The response calls for evaluations to evolve with each generation, but does not explain that advancing them quickly enables researchers to characterize new phenomena exhibited by more powerful models.

astra-6.text:
Because if our ability to evaluate these systems lags behind our ability to build and deploy them, we’re putting people into situations we don’t yet know how to assess. A system can become much more capable without becoming better for the people using it.

So we need to look beyond whether it gets an answer right. Does it help someone make an informed decision? Does it preserve their agency? What happens when someone uses it repeatedly, especially when they’re vulnerable? Those are harder questions than a conventional benchmark can capture, but they’re essential.

And as systems change, those evaluations have to change too. Otherwise, we risk treating yesterday’s tests as evidence that tomorrow’s systems are safe. The point is to make understanding human consequences part of the development process, early enough that it can actually shape what gets built.

r001.rationale: The response says evaluations must change as systems change, but does not explain that capability gains can saturate previously state-of-the-art evaluations.

r002.rationale: It does not say that AI systems can find ways around specific evaluations.

r003.rationale: It calls for evaluating changing systems and their human consequences, but does not explain that this enables researchers to characterize new phenomena exhibited by more powerful models.

sol-6.1.text:
Because the capabilities of these systems are moving faster than our ability to understand their effects on people. If our evaluations stay fixed while the technology changes, we can end up measuring what was important yesterday and missing what matters today.

With Humane Evals, the question has to go beyond whether a model gives a correct answer. Does it help someone make an informed decision? Does it preserve their agency? What happens when someone interacts with it repeatedly, especially if they’re vulnerable or seeking emotional support? Those effects may not show up in a single exchange.

We need the research to keep pace so that we can identify harms early and give developers meaningful feedback while they can still change the system. Otherwise, we’re learning about the consequences through people’s lives after deployment.

r001.rationale: It says evaluations can become outdated as technology changes, but does not explain that rapid capability gains can saturate previously state-of-the-art evaluations.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention AI systems finding ways around or circumventing specific evaluations.

r003.rationale: It calls for keeping research in pace to identify harms and assess effects, but does not say this enables researchers to characterize new phenomena exhibited by more powerful models.
